Welcome to the official documentation portal and report repository for Team-01 in the Software Defined Radio Laboratory course at the Department of Electrical Engineering.

Lab Portal Overview

This portal hosts all laboratory documentation, including pre-lab preparation, real-time measurement logs, raw .cf32 data analysis, downloadable PDF reports, and post-session analyses for ADALM-Pluto SDR experiments.

docs.title: Reproduce the offline results
docs.text:
From this directory, with Python 3 and the eight .cf32 files present:

python -m pip install numpy scipy matplotlib
python analyze_lab01.py

The script writes the three generated PNGs and lab01_results.json under images/. --data and --output accept alternative directories. The captures are little-endian interleaved float32 I/Q with no header. Existing names use Team_01; newly recorded files use Team-01. The archived filenames encode tuned RX LO in hertz, sample rate in samples per second, requested gain in dB, and capture timestamp. log.md maps every archived file to its role.

Regenerate the PDF from the editable source with python -m pip install markdown and python build_lab01_report.py. The renderer uses Chrome, Edge, or Chromium. Supply --browser PATH if your browser is installed elsewhere.

docs.title: Run and check the GNU Radio flowgraphs
docs.text:
Use GNU Radio 3.10 with Qt and gr-iio, such as the activated radioconda environment on Windows. Open lab01_monitor.grc for receive-only operation or lab01_loopback.grc for cabled loopback, then generate and run from GRC. The corresponding .py files are also runnable in the same environment.

grcc -o . lab01_monitor.grc lab01_loopback.grc
python -B check_recorder.py

The test uses a GNU Radio +100 kHz complex source, a Throttle and a finite stream. It also checks the exact sample cap, arming, capture-setting changes, file format and close on flowgraph stop. sdrlab_iq_recorder.py is the source for both GRC Embedded Python Blocks. After editing it, paste the complete source into each block and regenerate. Close the Qt window to stop cleanly. Use a fresh arm after a rate, LO or gain change. Recordings go in recordings/ under the working directory, capped at 80 MB or 4 s. A second capture with identical settings and the same timestamp uses the next unused timestamp to avoid overwriting evidence.

docs.title: Setup and device readback
docs.text:
Use LAN for IIO data and USB for power. Use RX1 for the antenna in monitor mode and leave TX1 empty. Stop the flowgraph before changing cabling. For the lab's cable-only loopback, follow the bench's approved attenuation setup, start at 60 dB TX attenuation, keep attenuation at or above 40 dB and manual RX gain at or below 10 dB. For the mobile uplink demonstration, keep the phone at least 5 m away and start at 0 dB RX gain. Run only one streaming app at a time.

ping 192.168.1.10
iio_attr -u ip:192.168.1.10 -C
iio_attr -u ip:192.168.1.10 -c ad9361-phy altvoltage0 frequency_available
iio_attr -u ip:192.168.1.10 -c ad9361-phy altvoltage0 frequency
iio_attr -u ip:192.168.1.10 -i -c ad9361-phy voltage0 sampling_frequency
iio_attr -u ip:192.168.1.10 -i -c ad9361-phy voltage0 rf_bandwidth
iio_attr -u ip:192.168.1.10 -i -c ad9361-phy voltage0 gain_control_mode
iio_attr -u ip:192.168.1.10 -i -c ad9361-phy voltage0 hardwaregain

Save console output during the acquisition. The installed GNU Radio 3.10.12 Pluto source generates set_filter_params('Off', …) but omits an RX bandwidth setter. The 20 MHz GRC field therefore needs a device readback. For 20 MS/s surveys, use a 1024-point FFT, Average = None, and clear Max Hold between steps. Use 2.6 MS/s for recording burst timing. The report identifies the specific hardware evidence that still needs to be captured.

docs.title: RF Spectrum Monitoring
docs.text:
SeyedParham Moghaddasi and Amirali Rajai · Team 01Archived acquisitions on 1 and 8 November 2026

Download the lab report (PDF)

The ADALM-Pluto recorded a 433.935 MHz key-fob signal, GSM900 downlink carriers and bursty GSM900 uplink activity. The key-fob recording contains 102 complete packets with a median duration of 26.8 ms and a median repetition interval of 34.7 ms. GSM frequency-correction bursts place the receiver's indicated frequency about 2.86 ppm high. The loopback screenshots show that changing the RX LO leaves the principal RF label near 434.250 MHz.

docs.title: 1. Setup and spectrum monitoring
docs.text:
The AD9363 is a direct-conversion transceiver. RX1 feeds an LNA, quadrature mixers, analog low-pass filters, 12-bit I/Q ADCs and digital decimation. The Zynq transfers the complex samples to GNU Radio over IIO. The bench configuration uses USB for power and LAN for samples (ip:192.168.1.10, laptop 192.168.1.20). In receive mode the antenna is on RX1. The loopback uses a cable from TX1 to RX1. Lab manual, pp. 1–7 · Analog Devices Pluto documentation

Setup item Flowgraph or archived evidence RX chain Pluto source → QT frequency, waterfall and time sinks, plus the I/Q recorder. Both frequency displays use f_tune = int(fc + lo_shift). Initial requested settings 945 MHz, 2.6 MS/s, 20 dB manual RX gain and lo_shift = 0. Other rates are 5, 10 and 20 MS/s. Quadrature, RF DC and BB DC corrections are enabled. RX bandwidth GRC specifies Off and 20 MHz. The installed 3.10.12 RX template omits a bandwidth setter. A device readback is needed to establish the actual RF bandwidth. Working gain Both 20 MS/s downlink screenshots show 30 dB. The 943.49 and 951.99 MHz captures at 30 dB peak at 0.198 and 0.271 in either I or Q, below the lab's 0.5 target. Device and retune evidence The saved settings and filenames give requested values. Unit model, firmware, serial, actual LO range and IIO readback are pending. The 945→947 MHz test should move the axis by 2 MHz while preserving RF labels. The 947 MHz screenshot is missing. Figure 1. Initial live views at 2.6 and 20 MS/s, then the saved time trace. At 945 MHz, the nominal displayed intervals are 943.7–946.3 MHz and 935–955 MHz. The time trace shows I and Q amplitudes within ±0.5 in that snapshot.

Q1. Reliable span and sweep step. The lab labels a complex FFT bin as RF = RX LO + baseband frequency. At an FFT size of 1,024 the bin widths are 2.54 and 19.53 kHz at 2.6 and 20 MS/s. Receiver filters and noise shaping affect the edges, while residual DC can affect the center. In quiet capture F, 5%-of-rate bins yield a median central floor of −126.5 dBFS/Hz. The outer bins are near −119.2 dBFS/Hz, 7.3 dB higher. The contiguous region within 3 dB of the central floor spans −0.40 to +0.40 times the sample rate. This gives a noise-flatness estimate of 80% and supports 16 MHz steps at 20 MS/s. The full FFT displays overlap by 4 MHz. The retained 16 MHz spans meet at their boundaries. This test characterizes noise flatness on capture F at 2.6 MS/s. A swept reference tone would quantify gain flatness across each rate.

Recording check. The initial file contains 8,454,144 samples (67,633,152 bytes), or 3.252 s at 2.6 MS/s. The remaining seven files each contain 10,000,000 samples (80,000,000 bytes). Each satisfies size = 8 × sample count. The draft's “about two seconds” was a procedure target with no matching saved capture. See the logbook for the file inventory.

docs.title: 2. Cabled loopback and LO shift
docs.text:
The TX branch generates a complex tone of amplitude 0.5 at 2.6 MS/s and upconverts it around 434.000 MHz. The RX LO is 434 MHz plus lo_shift. The flowgraph starts at 60 dB TX attenuation and 10 dB RX gain, with attenuation limited to 40–89 dB. Based on the manual's +7 dBm TX maximum, the conservative input budgets before cable loss are −53 dBm at 60 dB and −33 dBm at 40 dB, both below the lab's −10 dBm ceiling. The experiment calls for a cable-only TX path and stopping the graph before changing the cable. Lab manual, pp. 2 and 8–12

Figure 2. Original loopback displays. Upper row shows the ±250 kHz sign test. The next two rows show shifts of 0, +100, +200 and −200 kHz from left to right. The saved negative shift differs from the assigned −100 kHz.

Q3. Signed frequencies in I/Q. I and Q are sampled in quadrature. The positive and negative complex tones rotate in opposite directions and appear at 434.250 MHz on the right and 433.750 MHz on the left. Sampling I alone produces the same cosine for either sign, with symmetric FFT peaks at ±250 kHz. The zero-shift positive tone is about −55 dBFS on the display.

Q4. Peak labels and slopes. Display labels below were read against the tick marks. Values are approximate, particularly for weak peaks near the noise floor. The 433.996 MHz annotation in the +100 kHz image is a cursor readout. The main line itself aligns with 434.250 MHz.

RX LO shift (kHz) Main (MHz) Other discernible peaks (MHz) 0 434.250 Main dominates. Small features near the center and mirror are close to the noise floor. +100 434.250 433.850, 434.000, 434.100, 434.650 +200 434.250 433.450, 434.000, 434.200, 435.050, plus weak features near 433.69 and 434.14 −200 434.250 433.450, 433.800, 434.000

The fixed line at 434.250 MHz has slope 0 and is the known RF input. The weak line near 434.000 MHz also has slope 0, consistent with TX LO leakage at RX1. Peaks near 434.100, 434.200 and 433.800 MHz follow the RX LO with slope +1, consistent with residual DC. A TX-side image at 433.750 MHz would stay fixed. A receiver I/Q mirror obeys fimage = 2 × RX LO − fRF and has slope +2, with predicted labels of 433.750, 433.950, 434.150 and 433.350 MHz in the four rows. The weak +200 kHz feature near 434.14 MHz is a possible match. The prominent moving spurs have approximate slopes +4 and −4 in the positive-shift views, with the +4 branch consistent with 433.45 MHz at −200 kHz. Their motion indicates tuning-dependent artifacts. The screenshots leave their mechanism unresolved.

Q5. Common-reference cancellation. If both synthesizers and the sample clock share a scale factor (1 + ε), the physical beat frequency is (250 kHz − lo_shift) × (1 + ε). Dividing by the actual sample rate to obtain cycles/sample cancels the factor. The software then uses nominal sample rate and adds the nominal RX LO, so the RF label stays 434.250 MHz. An independent GSM base station has its own reference, so the same cancellation does not apply. The required +100 kHz-shift loopback I/Q file is missing. The 2.54 kHz display bins bound the screenshot comparison, while sub-bin loopback estimation and a raw spur classification remain pending. The optional DC correction toggle comparison was unrecorded.

docs.title: 3. Band scans and signal identification
docs.text:
For 20 MS/s survey steps, the manual specifies a 1,024-point Blackman–Harris FFT, averaging off, Max Hold for 15–20 s per step and clearing it on retune. The 943 and 959 MHz screenshots show their requested rate, centers and 30 dB gain. Their Max Hold checkboxes are clear, so they document live waterfall views. Offline Max Hold comes from the archived recordings and their actual durations. Lab manual, pp. 12–14

Band Required tuning Evidence and results A · 88–108 MHz Optional 96 and 112 MHz steps with extended tuning No FM acquisition in the archive. Pluto's documented default LO range is 325–3,800 MHz. The unit's range was unrecorded. B · 430–440 MHz 435 MHz at 20 MS/s, then 434.5 MHz at 2.6 MS/s Live Max Hold and a 3.846 s file at 435 MHz and 2.6 MS/s. The draft describes 434.5 MHz for the live step. The 20 MS/s Band B evidence is missing. C · 935–960 MHz 943 and 959 MHz at 20 MS/s, retained spans 935–951 and 951–967 MHz Both live steps are present. Narrow continuous and intermittent GSM channels coexist with persistent several-MHz-wide blocks in the first view. C-2 · 890–915 MHz 898 and 914 MHz at 20 MS/s, retained spans 890–906 and 906–922 MHz The 914 MHz file and a focused 907.99 MHz capture are present. The 898 MHz step and time-aligned call log are missing. Figure 3. Live GSM900 downlink sweep at 943 MHz (left) and 959 MHz (right). The 943 MHz waterfall shows two persistent wide blocks. The 959 MHz view overlaps part of the second block. The waterfall's displayed time scale is approximate at 20 MS/s. Figure 4. Band B Max Hold preserves the key-fob peak near 433.94 MHz at roughly −81 dBFS while the live trace is near the floor. The saved screen is a frequency-sink view. The raw-data waterfall is Figure 6.

Downlink. GSM900 uses a 200 kHz carrier raster and nominal 200 kHz channels. The persistent near-952.8 MHz signal is consistent with ARFCN 89 and has repeated frequency-correction tones. A weaker series of frequency-correction tones is consistent with ARFCN 86 at 952.2 MHz. Low power and intermittent activity characterize ARFCNs 85 and 87 in the focused capture, with possible traffic activity. The saved 958.99 MHz raw spectrum provides insufficient evidence for the original draft's claimed 959.804 MHz traffic carrier. 3GPP TS 45.005, §2

Uplink. The 907.99 MHz file contains bursts on a 200 kHz raster around 907.4, 907.8 and 908.2 MHz. The last has a 99% midpoint of 908.2014 MHz. Adding the nominal 45 MHz duplex spacing gives 953.2014 MHz, consistent with ARFCN 91 (953.200 MHz nominal downlink). This identifies a frequency pair. A time-aligned call log would be needed to tie bursts to the test handset. The file encodes 30 dB requested gain. The prescribed ≥5 m separation and 0 dB initial gain are unverified.

Q6. Continuous and transient behavior. Band C showed the most persistent occupancy. Band B packets and the sampled C-2 carriers appeared intermittently. Max Hold retained the highest level per bin across the observed FFT frames, so a packet remained visible after the live spectrum returned to its baseline. Max Hold still depends on which frames reach the display.

docs.title: 4. Five measured signals
docs.text:
The offline recreation of Table 7 uses a linear, 50%-overlapped Hann Welch PSD and an offline Max Hold envelope from the same recording. The recorder supplied 3.846 s per file, shorter than the manual's ≥20 s live Max Hold dwell. The offline PSD averages burst-on frames for the key fob, #85, #87 and uplink #91, and all frames for #89. FFT lengths were 32,768, 2,048, 2,048, 8,192 and 1,024, giving 0.079, 1.270, 1.270, 0.317 and 2.539 kHz bins. Each is smaller than one twentieth of its measured x-dB width.

Each x-dB width is fU − fL, with center (fL + fU)/2. We used x = 20 dB when the peak exceeded its local Max Hold floor by at least 26 dB and x = 6 dB otherwise. In row order, the measured separations were 50.9, 23.8, 21.8, 26.6 and 15.5 dB. Bin power was normalized to a unit-amplitude complex tone for dBFS. These FFT peaks depend on the window and detection interval. The live Band B trace was captured under different settings and timing, so it is listed as display evidence only.

Figure 5. Welch PSD and Max Hold by channel. For the overlay, Max Hold bin power is divided by the window's equivalent noise bandwidth. The shaded region encloses 99% of the estimated in-channel signal power. This calculation uses sample counts and frequency labels from the raw files.

For 99% occupied bandwidth, subtract the off-burst PSD or the local continuous-carrier floor in linear power. Clip negative residuals to zero and integrate within the chosen channel (90 kHz for the key fob, 200 kHz for GSM). The edges are at 0.5% and 99.5% cumulative power. Interpolating across the ±4 kHz RX DC region removes the narrow center artifact in #85. The key fob lies 25 kHz outside the nominal central 80% of the 435 MHz capture, with 230 kHz clearance to the FFT edge. Its frequency and timing are clear, and its level is sensitive to front-end response.

docs.title: Band B waterfall and probability of intercept (Q7)
docs.text:
Figure 6. Sample-indexed waterfall from the entire 3.846 s Band B file. Adjacent rows are pooled for display; detection uses each original frame. The detail plot shows repeated in-band power and threshold crossings.

Consecutive 4,096-sample frames at 2.6 MS/s give 1.575 ms time bins. The final partial frame is included in the waterfall. Summed power over 433.935 MHz ±25 kHz was compared with −60.6 dBFS, 13 dB above the first 0.3 s median. Keeping complete runs of at least 12 ms yields 102 packets, starting at 0.356 s. The median duration is 26.78 ms (5th–95th percentile 26.78–28.36 ms) and the median start-to-start interval is 34.66 ms (33.08–34.66 ms). Durations and intervals have about one frame of edge quantization. The repetitive structure continues through the end of the capture. Multiple packets can arise from one press, so the packet count cannot recover the number of button presses.

The original draft estimates one live sighting for every three presses, with no event log or pre-lab prediction preserved. The flowgraph refreshes every 100 ms and uses 0.394 ms FFT frames at 2.6 MS/s. For a single randomly phased packet, a frame-overlap model gives POI ≈ (26.78 + 0.394)/100 = 27.2%. The draft's rough 33% is about 6 percentage points higher. The model concerns one packet, while the observation concerns presses that may send trains. Repeated packets, transport continuity and display threshold affect the comparison. The live display has insufficient cadence to measure the 34.7 ms repetition directly.

docs.title: GSM carrier centers (Q2)
docs.text:
The initial 945 MHz raw file is dominated by broad energy, so the carrier-grid estimate uses the 951.99 MHz capture. GSM frequency-correction channel (FCCH) pulses provide a narrow tone at one quarter of the 270.833 ksymbol/s symbol rate, or +67.708 kHz above the assigned carrier. We detect narrow peaks, test the 51-frame GSM timing pattern, interpolate three FFT bins and subtract 67.708 kHz. The correction avoids using the PSD midpoint of a modulated or intermittently occupied channel as a precision frequency reference. 3GPP TS 45.004, §2

ARFCN Grid (MHz) Inferred label (MHz) Label error (kHz) Error (ppm) Matched pulses / adjacent intervals at expected cadence 84 951.8000 951.80278 +2.784 +2.925 6 / 1, weak candidate 86 952.2000 952.20273 +2.729 +2.866 63 / 51 89 952.8000 952.80273 +2.728 +2.863 82 / 81

For GSM900 downlink, fgrid = 935 + 0.2 × ARFCN in MHz. The two strong cadence matches give a mean label error of +2.86 ppm. Their robust within-carrier spreads are 80 and 5 Hz. With a conservative half-bin allowance of ±1.27 kHz (±1.34 ppm), report +2.86 ±1.4 ppm for the label and approximately −2.86 ±1.4 ppm for the receiver oscillator (an assumed accurate BTS). This is an engineering uncertainty estimate. Offsets are about 2.73 kHz, well inside the nominal ±25 ppm, equivalent to ±23.6 kHz at 945 MHz. Analog Devices Pluto specifications

docs.text:

Relative error is 100 × (measured − reference)/reference. The GSM reference in the width column is the nominal 200 kHz channel allocation. The manual lists about 250 kHz occupied, which uses different acquisition and integration assumptions. The 99% values here are explicitly channel-limited.

The B99 ranges vary only the integration width by ±10%. The resulting 10–32 kHz GSM changes quantify sensitivity to spectral tails and adjacent energy. For gated signals the mask also matters. For example #85 used 5.9% of frames, #87 14.2% and #91 4.6%. For #89 the whole recording was used. Noise subtraction and thresholds define the measurement, while the nominal allocation is a channel plan. The two confirmed BTS references imply about +1.24 kHz receiver label bias at 433.92 MHz. About 11.2 kHz of the key-fob B99 midpoint offset remains after this correction, which may include transmitter offset and its asymmetric spectrum. The transmitter tolerance is unknown.

docs.title: Wide signals and technology comparison (Q8)
docs.text:
The 943 MHz survey shows persistent, roughly flat blocks with display edges around 942.0–946.6 MHz and 947.0–951.6 MHz, each about 4.6 MHz wide by the screenshot axis. The 959 MHz view also shows the upper edge of the second block. These visual estimates have about ±0.2 MHz width uncertainty from choosing boundaries in the color transitions. The 2.6 MS/s recordings at 943.49, 945.00 and 951.99 MHz sample different portions, and the receiver response shapes their edges. The full blocks lack a common raw span for Bx or B99. A width of 4.6 MHz differs by about +2% from the 4.5 MHz LTE resource span and −2% from the 4.68 MHz UMTS theoretical filter support, smaller than the visual uncertainty.

For systematic identification, acquire both shoulders in the reliable span at the same gain. Average power linearly and compare the roll-off on both sides, then inspect multiple waterfall rows at light and heavy load. A 5 MHz LTE carrier has 25 resource blocks, or 300 × 15 kHz = 4.5 MHz scheduled subcarrier span, with relatively steep edges and variable resource use. UMTS FDD uses 3.84 Mcps and root-raised-cosine shaping with α = 0.22, giving rounded shoulders and theoretical support of about 4.68 MHz. Its continuously transmitted downlink and traffic-related power changes also appear in the waterfall. Width and persistence alone permit either service. The sharper block shoulders suggest LTE as a working hypothesis for both observed blocks. A matched, full-width recording is needed to compare slopes reliably. 3GPP TS 36.104 · 3GPP TS 25.104

The expected key fob, narrow GSM downlink and bursty uplink were present. The wide candidates were also present on the downlink display. A narrow 959.804 MHz traffic carrier could not be established from the upper-band recording. The beyond-band capture is useful as a quiet reference. Optional FM was outside the documented default tuning range.

docs.title: 7. Verification and follow-up
docs.text: Figure 7. Raw survey PSDs with the central 80% shaded. The 20 MS/s uplink recording supports frequency-domain survey measurements. Timing analysis uses 2.6 MS/s recordings. The wide downlink detail fills much of its recording, while the 967.99 MHz capture provides a quiet-span check. Item Finding and follow-up LO-shift readout The +100 kHz cursor annotation led to an incorrect draft peak label. Read the plotted line against the RF ticks, and save a matching raw file to resolve the moving spurs. Missing 959.8 MHz traffic peak Raw capture G shows a weak upper downlink and narrow features around and above 960 MHz. Verify the intended LO and timing before assigning a traffic channel. Edge noise and bandwidth The quiet file shows a 7.3 dB edge rise. Crop to the central 80% for sweeps. Save actual analog bandwidth readback because the installed RX template does not write the GRC value. IIO discovery or busy message The original draft lists these symptoms with no saved console log. The manual's recovery is to check the LAN URI and close concurrent Pluto streaming applications.

docs.title: What we would do differently
docs.text:
1. Save device identification, the five IIO attribute readbacks and paired 945/947 MHz screenshots before sweeping. Log the working-gain progression and the roles of both team members.
  2. Save the +100 kHz-shift loopback I/Q and exact −100 kHz screen before reconnecting the antenna. Check sample counts and tone frequency on the bench while there is time to repeat the shot.
  3. Use separate rate settings for the wide captures and burst timing. Keep both wide-block edges inside a single reliable 20 MS/s span and record two narrow captures at different LO settings to test artifacts.
  4. Save 20 s Max Hold traces, the 435 MHz 20 MS/s view, the 898 MHz uplink step and time-stamped press/call counts. Log the uplink distance and initial gain when dialing.

The accompanying README includes the commands to reproduce the offline analyses and read the device. Both flowgraphs compile under GNU Radio 3.10.12. The recorder's checks cover the exact sample cap, rearming, metadata changes, stop and a generated +100 kHz tone. The checks used a GNU Radio signal source without a connected Pluto. The archive includes the Markdown report, flowgraphs, generated Python, recorder code, eight raw files and reconstructed logbook.

AI disclosure. OpenAI Codex helped revise the report, debug the recorder, implement the offline calculations and describe provisional interpretations. Figures and calculations are reproducible from Team 01's recordings. Course regulations §5-7 reserve interpretation and conclusions for the team. The authors should independently check the generated analysis and write their own interpretations before submission.

docs.title: Lab 01 logbook — Team 01
docs.text:

docs.title: 1. Summary of Theoretical Concepts
docs.text: RF receiver architectures are bounded at lower signal levels by thermal and internal component noise, and at upper levels by non-linear gain saturation and intermodulation distortion.

docs.title: Noise Figure (NF) and Noise Temperature (Te)
docs.text:
The Noise Factor (\(F\)) and Noise Figure (\(NF\)) measure the degradation of the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (\(SNR\)) as a signal propagates through a receiver processing chain:

\[F = \frac{SNR_{\text{in}}}{SNR_{\text{out}}} = 1 + \frac{T_e}{T_0}, \quad NF = 10 \log_{10}(F)\]

The input-referred noise floor (\(N_{\text{floor}}\)) over bandwidth \(B\) is expressed as:

\[N_{\text{floor}} = -174\text{ dBm/Hz} + NF + 10 \log_{10}(B)\]

docs.title: Y-Factor Noise Measurement Method
docs.text:
The Y-Factor method utilizes a calibrated noise source operating in two states: OFF (\(T_c \approx T_0\)) and ON (\(T_h \gg T_0\)), defined by Excess Noise Ratio (\(ENR\)):

\[ENR = \frac{T_h - T_0}{T_0}, \quad Y = \frac{T_h + T_e}{T_0 + T_e} \implies F = \frac{ENR - Y \left(\frac{T_c}{T_0} - 1\right)}{Y - 1}\]

docs.title: Third-Order Intercept Point (IIP3) and Gain Compression (P1dB)
docs.text: Under two-tone excitation at \(f_1\) and \(f_2\), 3rd-order non-linearities generate intermodulation products (IM3) at \(2f_1 - f_2\) and \(2f_2 - f_1\).

docs.title: 2. Theoretical Analysis Highlights
docs.text:
• Frontend Filter Relocation (Question 1c): Relocating the \(3\text{ dB}\) filter to the frontend alters Friis chain hierarchy (Stage 1 = Filter, Stage 2 = LNA, Stage 3 = Mixer/ADC), resulting in \(NF_{\text{new}} \approx 4.95\text{ dB}\).
  • General Y-Factor Relation (Question 2a): Exact derivation for \(T_c \neq T_0\) yields \(F = \frac{ENR - Y (T_c/T_0 - 1)}{Y - 1}\).

docs.title: Y-Factor Simulation Results (\(lab02\_sim.grc\))
docs.text:

  • Design Note: At low gain, \(Y = 0.30\text{ dB} < 3\text{ dB}\) amplifies readout error sensitivity, justifying the requirement for an \(ENR \approx 35\text{ dB}\) source per Table 4 design.

Download Full Report (PDF)

Report Overview

This report presents the analytical findings, experimental data tables, visual curve interpretations, and answers to all core and expansion questions for Laboratory 2: RF Noise Figure and Linearity Parameters. Measurements were acquired using the dual ADALM-PLUTO SDR testbench via lab02_combined.grc and lab02_antenna_response_gui.py.

docs.title: 1. Device Noise Floor and Direct Method (Table 3 & Question 1)
docs.text:
In digital SDR architectures, internal power is represented in decibels relative to digital full-scale (\(\text{dBFS}\)). Converting digital power readings into absolute analog power in \(\text{dBm}\) at the receiver input port requires the calibrated full-scale conversion factor \(G_{FS}\):

\[P_{\text{in}}\,[\text{dBm}] = P_{\text{digital}}\,[\text{dBFS}] - G_{FS}\]

For the ADALM-PLUTO receiver under the baseline calibrated manual gain setting of rf_gain = 40.2 dB, the nominal conversion factor is \(G_{FS} = 20.0\text{ dB}\), establishing that \(0\text{ dBFS}\) corresponds to \(-20.0\text{ dBm}\) of analog input power.

docs.title: Experimental Calibration Data (Table 3)
docs.text:
With the receiver input SMA port left open (unconnected termination), baseline digital noise power \(N_{\text{off}}\) was acquired across three gain settings using the wideband noise channel filter (\(B_n \approx 400\text{ kHz}\)). The direct noise figure is estimated via:

\[\text{NF}_{\text{direct}}\,[\text{dB}] \approx N_{\text{off}}\,[\text{dBFS}] - G_{FS} - 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{B_n}{1\text{ Hz}}\right) - (-174\text{ dBm/Hz}) \approx N_{\text{off}}\,[\text{dBFS}] + 97.98\text{ dB}\] Parameter / Quantity rf_gain = 29.7 dB rf_gain = 40.2 dB rf_gain = 49.6 dB Open-Port Noise Power \(N_{\text{off}}\) [dBFS] \(-73.50\) \(-74.20\) \(-66.20\) Direct Noise Figure \(\text{NF}_{\text{direct}}\) [dB] \(24.48\) \(23.78\) \(31.78\)

At lower front-end gains (\(29.7\text{ dB}\) and \(40.2\text{ dB}\)), the measured digital noise power hovers at \(\approx -74\text{ dBFS}\), which is set by internal ADC quantization noise and digital baseband noise. At the maximum gain of \(49.6\text{ dB}\), the amplified analog front-end thermal noise overcomes the ADC quantization floor, causing the digital reading to rise to \(-66.20\text{ dBFS}\). Because the direct estimation formula presumes a static conversion factor \(G_{FS} = 20\text{ dB}\) regardless of gain, it produces an erroneous apparent NF increase at \(49.6\text{ dB}\), demonstrating why the direct method fails under varying front-end gain conditions.

docs.title: Question 1: Direct Method vs. \(Y\)-Factor Method Requirements
docs.text:
Prompt

What quantities does the direct method require that the \(Y\)-Factor method does not?

Answer: The direct method depends strictly on knowing three absolute system parameters:

  1. Absolute Conversion Factor / Gain (\(G_{FS}\)): The precise hardware gain and full-scale calibration linking \(\text{dBFS}\) to \(\text{dBm}\). Any systematic calibration inaccuracy in \(G_{FS}\) creates an identical, dB-for-dB error in the extracted noise figure.
  2. Equivalent Noise Bandwidth (\(B_n\)): The exact integrated brick-wall noise bandwidth of the digital FIR channel filter.
  3. Absolute Thermal Noise Power Reference: Explicit calibration against the theoretical input thermal noise density \(k T_0 = -174\text{ dBm/Hz}\) at reference temperature \(T_0 = 290\text{ K}\).

In contrast, the \(Y\)-Factor method relies exclusively on a relative power ratio \(Y = N_{\text{on}} / N_{\text{off}}\) and the known Excess Noise Ratio (\(\text{ENR}\)) of the noise source. Because internal receiver gain, filter bandwidth, and digital scale factors affect \(N_{\text{on}}\) and \(N_{\text{off}}\) identically, they cancel completely out of \(Y\), rendering the \(Y\)-Factor method independent of receiver gain, filter bandwidth, and digital scale calibrations.

docs.title: 2. Noise Figure via the \(Y\)-Factor Method (Table 4 & Question 2)
docs.text:
Broadband Gaussian noise generated by the transmitting PLUTO SDR was injected into the receiver port through a fixed \(30\text{ dB}\) external safety pad (\(A_{\text{pad}} = 30\text{ dB}\)). Under nominal transmitter attenuation (\(A_{tx} = 58.5\text{ dB}\)), the effective excess noise ratio referenced to the receiver input is:

\[ \text{ENR}_{\text{eff}} = 73.4 - A_{tx} = 73.4 - 58.5 \approx 15.0\text{ dB} \]

The \(Y\)-factor and receiver noise figure are computed via:

\[ Y\,[\text{dB}] = N_{\text{on}}\,[\text{dBFS}] - N_{\text{off}}\,[\text{dBFS}] \] \[ \text{NF}\,[\text{dB}] = \text{ENR}_{\text{eff}}\,[\text{dB}] - 10\log_{10}\!\left(10^{Y\,[\text{dB}]/10} - 1\right) \]

docs.text:
Test Frequency rf_gain = 29.7 dB rf_gain = 40.2 dB rf_gain = 49.6 dB 434 MHz \(N_{\text{on}} = -72.60\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 0.90\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 21.38\text{ dB}}\) \(N_{\text{on}} = -67.60\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 6.60\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 9.47\text{ dB}}\) \(N_{\text{on}} = -59.20\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 7.00\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 8.97\text{ dB}}\) 834 MHz \(N_{\text{on}} = -72.70\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 0.80\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 21.94\text{ dB}}\) \(N_{\text{on}} = -69.10\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 5.10\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 11.51\text{ dB}}\) \(N_{\text{on}} = -60.50\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 5.70\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 10.66\text{ dB}}\) 1234 MHz \(N_{\text{on}} = -72.30\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 1.20\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 19.97\text{ dB}}\) \(N_{\text{on}} = -68.30\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 5.90\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 10.39\text{ dB}}\) \(N_{\text{on}} = -59.70\text{ dBFS}\)\(Y = 6.50\text{ dB}\)\(\mathbf{NF = 9.60\text{ dB}}\)

As predicted by Friis' formula for cascaded noise figure, reducing receiver front-end gain degrades noise performance severely (rising from \(\approx 9.0\text{ dB}\) at high gain to \(> 21\text{ dB}\) at low gain). When front-end RF gain is low, the noise contribution of the mixer, baseband PGAs, and downstream ADC quantization noise dominates the receiver cascade.

docs.title: Question 2: Limits on \(Y\)-Factor and Error Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text:
Prompt

Why should \(Y\) be neither too small nor too large? For the smallest \(Y\) in your table, calculate the effect of a \(0.1\text{ dB}\) reading error on the calculated noise figure.

Answer:

  • Why \(Y\) cannot be too small (\(Y < 3\text{ dB}\)): As \(Y \to 0\text{ dB}\) (\(Y_{\text{linear}} \to 1\)), the denominator \((10^{Y/10}-1) \to 0\). In this regime, \(\vert{}d\text{NF}/dY\vert{}\) diverges toward infinity, meaning minute measurement noise or instrument flicker produces extreme errors in computed noise figure.
  • Why \(Y\) cannot be too large (\(Y > 15\text{ dB}\)): An excessively large \(Y\) requires high injected noise power that drives receiver mixers, baseband filters, and ADCs into non-linear compression during the ON state, violating the prerequisite of linear operation.

Mathematical Error Sensitivity Derivation: Differentiating \(\text{NF} = \text{ENR} - 10\log_{10}(10^{Y/10}-1)\) with respect to \(Y\) (in decibels):

\[ \frac{d\text{NF}}{dY} = -\frac{10^{Y/10}}{10^{Y/10}-1} = -\frac{1}{1 - 10^{-Y/10}} \]

Taking the smallest measured \(Y\)-factor in Table 4 (\(Y = 0.80\text{ dB}\) at \(834\text{ MHz}\), rf_gain = 29.7 dB):

\[ 10^{-0.80/10} = 10^{-0.08} \approx 0.8318 \] \[ \left|\frac{d\text{NF}}{dY}\right| = \frac{1}{1 - 0.8318} = \frac{1}{0.1682} \approx 5.94\text{ dB/dB} \]

Therefore, an instrument reading error of merely \(\delta Y = \pm 0.10\text{ dB}\) induces a large noise figure error of:

\[ \delta\text{NF} \approx 5.94 \times 0.10\text{ dB} \approx \pm 0.59\text{ dB} \]

By contrast, for \(Y = 6.60\text{ dB}\) (rf_gain = 40.2 dB), the sensitivity factor is only \(|d\text{NF}/dY| \approx 1.28\), meaning a \(0.1\text{ dB}\) error shifts NF by just \(\pm 0.13\text{ dB}\).

docs.title: 3. Single-Tone Power Sweep and \(P_{1\text{dB}}\) Compression (Table 5 & Question 3)
docs.text:
A single sinusoidal test tone at \(f_1 = f_c + 300\text{ kHz}\) was applied at rf_gain = 40.2 dB. Transmitter attenuation \(A_{tx}\) was stepped from \(60\text{ dB}\) down to \(40\text{ dB}\). Input power is determined from:

\[ P_{\text{in}}\,[\text{dBm}] = -35.5 - A_{tx} \] \[ P_{\text{in}}\,[\text{dBFS}] = P_{\text{in}}\,[\text{dBm}] + G_{FS} = -15.5 - A_{tx} \]

docs.title: Extracted Compression Parameters
docs.text:
• Small-Signal Linear Gain (\(G_0\)): \(59.0\text{ dB}\) (averaged across the linear region \(A_{tx} = 60\text{ dB}\) to \(53\text{ dB}\)).
  • 1-dB Gain Compression Point (\(G = G_0 - 1 = 58.0\text{ dB}\)): Occurs between \(-68.5\text{ dBFS}\) and \(-65.5\text{ dBFS}\). Interpolating yields:
\[ \text{Input } P_{1\text{dB}} \approx -66.5\text{ dBFS} \quad (-86.5\text{ dBm}) \]
  • Output Level at 1-dB Compression: \(-8.0\text{ dBFS}\).
  • Clipping Plateau: For \(P_{\text{in}} > -57.5\text{ dBFS}\), output tone power clamps at a fixed ceiling of \(-6.50\text{ dBFS}\).

docs.title: Question 3: Output Level at Compression and Primary Limiting Mechanism
docs.text:
Prompt

At the compression point, what was the output level in dBFS? What do you conclude regarding the limiting factor (ADC vs. analog stages)?

Answer: At the 1-dB compression point, the measured fundamental output level was \(-8.0\text{ dBFS}\). For higher input drives, the output power saturates abruptly into a hard plateau at \(-6.50\text{ dBFS}\).

  • In purely analog RF stages (e.g., LNA or passive mixer saturation), gain compression rolls off smoothly and progressively over a wide dynamic range (\(> 15\text{ dB}\)).
  • In this receiver, the transfer curve exhibits sharp, abrupt saturation within a few decibels of digital full scale (\(0\text{ dBFS}\)).

Conclusion: The dominant physical limiting factor is digital ADC full-scale clipping and baseband programmable gain amplifier (PGA) saturation, rather than analog front-end LNA compression.

docs.title: 4. Two-Tone Intermodulation Test and \(\text{IIP}_3\) (Table 6 & Questions 4, 5)
docs.text:
Two equal-amplitude tones were injected at \(f_1 = f_c + 300\text{ kHz}\) and \(f_2 = f_c + 400\text{ kHz}\) (\(\Delta f = 100\text{ kHz}\)) at rf_gain = 40.2 dB. Input tone power was swept from \(-70.0\text{ dBFS}\) to \(-54.0\text{ dBFS}\). The intermodulation distance is \(\Delta = P_{\text{fund}} - P_{\text{IMD3}}\), and the input third-order intercept point is computed as:

\[ \text{IIP}_3 = P_{\text{in}} + \frac{\Delta}{2} \]

docs.title: Regression and Intercept Parameters
docs.text:
• Fundamental Output Tone Slope: \(0.97\text{ dB/dB} \approx 1.0\text{ dB/dB}\) (confirming linear transfer gain).
  • Measured \(\text{IMD}_3\) Product Slope: \(1.10\text{ dB/dB}\).
  • Mean Calculated \(\text{IIP}_3\): \(-53.8\text{ dBFS}\) (\(-73.8\text{ dBm}\)).
  • Intercept-to-Compression Distance: \(\text{IIP}_3 - P_{1\text{dB}} = -53.8 - (-66.5) = +12.7\text{ dB}\).

docs.title: Question 4: Measured \(\text{IMD}_3\) Slope and Validity of \(\text{IIP}_3\)
docs.text:
Prompt

What was the measured slope of the third-order intermodulation products? If it differs from 3, what conclusion do you draw regarding the nonlinear mechanism, and what is the validity of your \(\text{IIP}_3\) value?

Answer: The measured \(\text{IMD}_3\) product slope is \(1.10\text{ dB/dB}\), which departs markedly from the theoretical weakly nonlinear slope of \(3.0\text{ dB/dB}\).

  1. Nonlinear Mechanism: This slope anomaly demonstrates that intermodulation is not generated solely by receiver internal small-signal third-order Taylor polynomial distortion. As documented in the troubleshooting guide (Table 9 of the manual), when the transmitting PLUTO SDR operates near full output scale, its transmitted output already contains source-generated intermodulation products that scale \(\approx 1:1\) with transmit power. Furthermore, digital ADC clipping introduces piecewise-linear threshold distortion that does not follow power-series mathematics.
  2. Validity of \(\text{IIP}_3\): Because the fundamental premise of a \(3:1\) intercept slope is violated, the calculated value of \(\text{IIP}_3 = -53.8\text{ dBFS}\) cannot be interpreted as an ideal asymptotic small-signal third-order intercept point. Rather, it represents an apparent or empirical intercept metric valid only within the specific testing window.

docs.title: Question 5: Comparison of \(\text{IIP}_3 - P_{1\text{dB}}\) with \(9.6\text{ dB}\) and Peak Envelope Dynamics
docs.text:
Prompt

Compare \(\text{IIP}_3 - P_{1\text{dB}}\) with \(9.6\text{ dB}\). Why does compression begin earlier in two-tone tests than in single-tone tests?

Answer:

  • Numerical Comparison: The measured difference is \(\text{IIP}_3 - P_{1\text{dB}} = +12.7\text{ dB}\), which is moderately higher than the canonical \(9.6\text{ dB}\) offset predicted for an ideal memoryless third-order polynomial nonlinearity, due to non-ideal slope compression and ADC clipping dynamics.
  • Why Two-Tone Compression Occurs Earlier: In a single-tone excitation of voltage amplitude \(V_0\), peak instantaneous voltage is \(V_{\text{peak}} = V_0\), giving peak envelope power \(\text{PEP} = V_0^2 / (2R) = P_{\text{avg}}\). In a two-tone test where each tone has amplitude \(V_0\), constructive interference occurs whenever the carriers align in phase:
\[ V_{\text{peak, 2-tone}} = V_0 + V_0 = 2 V_0 \]

Because instantaneous electrical power scales quadratically with voltage (\(V^2\)), peak envelope power is:

\[ \text{PEP} \propto (2 V_0)^2 = 4 V_0^2 \implies +6.0\text{ dB higher than a single tone of equal amplitude} \]

Consequently, the composite envelope reaches the receiver ADC full-scale saturation limit 6 dB earlier in per-tone input power than a single-tone stimulus.

docs.text:
1. Primary Operational Passband (\(1.65\text{ GHz} - 1.76\text{ GHz}\)): A dominant, smooth global resonance peak reaches \(-28.80\text{ dB}\) at \(1.70\text{ GHz}\). The extracted 3-dB bandwidth of \(110.0\text{ MHz}\) yields a fractional bandwidth of \(\text{FBW} = (110 / 1700) \times 100\% \approx 6.5\%\), typical of a tuned half-wave dipole or matched blade monopole antenna.
  2. Secondary Multi-Band Resonant Peaks:
    • Sub-1 GHz Cellular Peak (\(\approx 1.02\text{ GHz}\)): A distinct local peak reaches \(\approx -31.8\text{ dB}\) near \(1.0\text{ GHz}\), matching the commercial GSM-900 / LTE cellular mobile uplink band.
    • 2.4 GHz ISM Band Peak (\(\approx 2.44\text{ GHz}\)): A pronounced resonance peak reaches \(\approx -33.5\text{ dB}\) across the \(2.40 - 2.48\text{ GHz}\) ISM band (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth), confirming a multi-band commercial design.
  3. Electrically Small Mismatch Fluctuations (\(< 900\text{ MHz}\)): Below \(900\text{ MHz}\), the curve exhibits severe rapid fluctuations and deep nulls plunging down to \(-73\text{ dB}\) at \(\approx 550\text{ MHz}\). At these low frequencies (\(\lambda \approx 50 - 75\text{ cm}\)), the antenna is electrically small (\(l \ll \lambda/2\)), causing severe impedance mismatch (\(\Gamma \approx 1\)) and negligible radiation efficiency.
  4. High-Frequency Path Loss Rolloff (\(> 2.5\text{ GHz}\)): Beyond the \(2.44\text{ GHz}\) ISM peak, received power drops monotonically down to \(-63\text{ dB}\) at \(3.0\text{ GHz}\), following Friis free-space path loss (\(\propto f^2\)) compounded by SMA coaxial dielectric losses.

docs.title: Question 6: Variation Rates of Noise Figure and \(P_{1\text{dB}}\) with Gain
docs.text:
Prompt

Tabulate Noise Figure and \(P_{1\text{dB}}\) as a function of gain. At what rate (dB per dB of gain) does each metric vary?

Answer:

  • \(P_{1\text{dB}}\) Variation Rate: Across all gain transitions, input \(P_{1\text{dB}}\) shifts downward at exactly the rate of gain increase:
\[ \frac{\Delta P_{1\text{dB}}}{\Delta \text{Gain}} = -1.0\text{ dB / dB gain} \]

Because the output clipping ceiling is fixed by the ADC full-scale rail, every \(1\text{ dB}\) of added front-end gain reduces the allowable input power by exactly \(1\text{ dB}\).

  • Noise Figure (NF) Variation Rate:
    • From \(29.7\text{ dB}\) to \(40.2\text{ dB}\) (\(\Delta \text{Gain} = +10.5\text{ dB}\)): \(\Delta \text{NF} = -11.91\text{ dB} \implies \mathbf{-1.13\text{ dB / dB gain}}\) (rapid sensitivity improvement as LNA gain suppresses ADC quantization noise).
    • From \(40.2\text{ dB}\) to \(49.6\text{ dB}\) (\(\Delta \text{Gain} = +9.4\text{ dB}\)): \(\Delta \text{NF} = -0.50\text{ dB} \implies \mathbf{-0.05\text{ dB / dB gain}}\) (plateauing near the LNA's intrinsic noise figure).

docs.title: Question 7: Maximum Dynamic Range and Blocker Tolerance
docs.text:
Prompt

At which gain is dynamic range (\(P_{1\text{dB}} - N_{\text{floor}}\)) maximized? Which gain setting should be chosen to receive a weak signal in the presence of a strong adjacent blocker, and why?

Answer:

  1. Maximum Dynamic Range: Both linear dynamic range (\(38.0\text{ dB}\)) and Spurious-Free Dynamic Range (\(\text{SFDR} = 33.8\text{ dB}\)) reach their global peak at the nominal gain setting of \(40.2\text{ dB}\).
  2. Weak Signal Reception with Strong Adjacent Blocker: Select the nominal or lower gain setting (\(40.2\text{ dB}\) or lower), and never maximum gain (\(49.6\text{ dB}\)). At maximum gain, input \(P_{1\text{dB}}\) collapses to \(-76.0\text{ dBFS}\) (\(-96.0\text{ dBm}\)); a strong adjacent blocker would immediately overdrive the receiver into hard ADC clipping, generating reciprocal mixing and cross-modulation distortion that blinds the receiver. Nominal gain preserves \(10\text{ dB}\) more linearity headroom while maintaining near-optimum noise figure.

docs.title: 7. Mandatory Analyses, Expansion Question 8, and Error Breakdown
Mandatory Analysis 1: NF and Linearity vs. Gain (SFDR Argument)
docs.text: Plotting NF and \(\text{IIP}_3\) against receiver gain exhibits two opposing trends. Below \(40\text{ dB}\) gain, NF improves sharply (\(\approx -1.13\text{ dB/dB}\)) while linearity degrades at \(-1.0\text{ dB/dB}\). Above \(40\text{ dB}\) gain, NF reaches diminishing returns (\(\approx -0.05\text{ dB/dB}\)), but linearity continues to degrade at \(-1.0\text{ dB/dB}\). The optimal trade-off lies at rf_gain = 40.2 dB, where \(\text{SFDR} = 33.8\text{ dB}\) is maximized.

docs.title: Mandatory Analysis 2: Input-Output Transfer Characteristics
docs.text: In single-tone mode, fundamental output power tracks input drive linearly (\(G_0 = 59.0\text{ dB}\)) until 1-dB compression occurs at \(P_{\text{in}} = -66.5\text{ dBFS}\), clamping hard at \(-6.50\text{ dBFS}\). In two-tone mode, constructive peak envelope alignment produces early saturation, with the empirical intercept point at \(\text{IIP}_3 = -53.8\text{ dBFS}\) (\(+12.7\text{ dB}\) above \(P_{1\text{dB}}\)).

docs.title: Mandatory Analysis 3: Direct Method vs. \(Y\)-Factor Comparison
docs.text: Comparing Table 3 and Table 4 confirms that the direct method matches physical reality only at the calibrated nominal gain (rf_gain = 40.2 dB). At \(49.6\text{ dB}\), the direct formula yields an erroneous NF increase to \(31.78\text{ dB}\) because amplified analog noise overrides ADC quantization noise while assuming static \(G_{FS} = 20\text{ dB}\). The \(Y\)-factor method correctly tracks physical behavior, confirming an actual NF reduction to \(8.97\text{ dB}\).

docs.title: Question 8 (Expansion Question): Why Increasing Gain Does Not Continuously Improve Sensitivity
docs.text:
Prompt

Why does increasing receiver gain not continuously improve sensitivity? Quantify your answer using your experimental data.

Answer: Receiver sensitivity is governed by the minimum detectable input signal power \(S_{\text{min}}\):

\[ S_{\text{min}}\,[\text{dBm}] = -174\text{ dBm/Hz} + \text{NF}\,[\text{dB}] + 10\log_{10}(B) + \text{SNR}_{\text{min}}\,[\text{dB}] \]

Sensitivity depends directly on the Noise Figure (\(\text{NF}\)), not on gain. Gain amplifies both signal and input thermal noise equally, preserving SNR. According to Friis' cascaded noise formula:

\[ F_{\text{total}} = F_{\text{LNA}} + \frac{F_{\text{mixer}}-1}{G_{\text{LNA}}} + \frac{F_{\text{ADC}}-1}{G_{\text{LNA}} G_{\text{mixer}}} \]

Once \(G_{\text{LNA}}\) is large enough to suppress downstream noise contributions, \(F_{\text{total}} \to F_{\text{LNA}}\) asymptotically.

  • Quantitative Evidence:
    • Increasing gain from \(29.7\text{ dB}\) to \(40.2\text{ dB}\) (\(+10.5\text{ dB}\)) reduces NF by \(11.91\text{ dB}\) (from \(21.38\text{ dB}\) to \(9.47\text{ dB}\)), improving sensitivity by nearly \(12\text{ dB}\).
    • Increasing gain from \(40.2\text{ dB}\) to \(49.6\text{ dB}\) (\(+9.4\text{ dB}\)) reduces NF by merely \(0.50\text{ dB}\) (from \(9.47\text{ dB}\) to \(8.97\text{ dB}\)).
  • Linearity Penalty: Simultaneously, input \(P_{1\text{dB}}\) degrades by \(9.5\text{ dB}\) (from \(-86.5\text{ dBm}\) to \(-96.0\text{ dBm}\)) and SFDR drops by \(6.0\text{ dB}\).

docs.title: 1. Why FM is More Immune to Noise than AM
docs.text:
In Amplitude Modulation (AM), information is encoded directly into the instantaneous amplitude of the high-frequency carrier. Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) from the channel adds algebraically to this envelope, making it mathematically impossible to eliminate noise without altering the original message.

Conversely, in Frequency Modulation (FM), the envelope amplitude remains strictly constant (\(A\)), and the message is encoded entirely within the instantaneous phase and frequency:

\[ s(t) = A \cos\!\big(2\pi f_c t + \varphi(t)\big) \]

This structural property provides two fundamental noise-rejection mechanisms:

  1. Amplitude Hard-Limiting: A receiver limiter (or in discrete SDR, taking the angular phase \(\arg(\cdot)\)) strips away all spurious amplitude variations caused by channel fading, atmospheric interference, and thermal noise without distorting the underlying message.
  2. Bandwidth-for-SNR Trade-Off: Above threshold, the post-detection output signal-to-noise ratio (\(\text{SNR}_o\)) scales quadratically with the frequency deviation ratio \((\Delta f / W)^2\):
\[ \text{SNR}_o \propto \left(\frac{\Delta f}{W}\right)^2 \text{CNR} \]

Increasing the frequency deviation widens the occupied spectrum, which in turn drastically suppresses detected baseband noise.

docs.title: 2. The Cost of the FM Advantage
docs.text:
The superior noise rejection of FM is traded directly against substantial radio spectrum consumption. According to Carson's bandwidth rule:

\[ B_T \approx 2(\Delta f + f_{\max}) \]

While a standard AM voice transmission occupies only \(2W \approx 10\text{ kHz}\), commercial Wideband FM (WFM) allocates roughly \(200\text{ kHz}\) per broadcast channel—an approximately twentyfold increase in spectrum usage.

docs.title: 3. The Threshold Effect and Catastrophic Breakdown
docs.text:
The quadratic noise suppression in FM holds only when the input Carrier-to-Noise Ratio (\(\text{CNR}\)) exceeds a critical threshold (\(\text{CNR}_{\text{th}} \approx 10\text{ dB}\)). When \(\text{CNR}\) falls below this boundary:

  • The noise phasor occasionally exceeds the carrier phasor in magnitude, sweeping the resultant vector around the origin and inducing a full \(2\pi\) phase wrap-around (phase slip).
  • Because the discriminator differentiates phase to extract audio, this rapid \(2\pi\) step manifests as a sharp Dirac-like impulse in time, heard as an audible "click" or "pop".
  • As the signal weakens further, the arrival rate of clicks accelerates exponentially, destroying phase coherence and driving the output \(\text{SNR}_o\) into a steep, catastrophic cliff. Unlike AM, where audio degrades gradually into background static, an FM signal drops off abruptly from near-flawless fidelity into complete unintelligibility.

docs.title: 1. Single-Tone Bessel Expansion and Carson's Bandwidth
docs.text:
For a single-tone message \(m(t) = \cos(2\pi f_m t)\), the instantaneous phase is:

\[ \varphi(t) = 2\pi\Delta f \int_0^t \cos(2\pi f_m \tau)\,d\tau = \frac{\Delta f}{f_m} \sin(2\pi f_m t) = \beta \sin(2\pi f_m t) \]

where \(\beta = \frac{\Delta f}{f_m}\) is the modulation index. The real bandpass signal is expressed as:

\[ s(t) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left\{ A e^{j(2\pi f_c t + \beta \sin(2\pi f_m t))} \right\} = A \cdot \operatorname{Re}\!\left\{ e^{j 2\pi f_c t} \cdot e^{j \beta \sin(2\pi f_m t)} \right\} \]

Applying the Jacobi-Anger expansion identity:

\[ e^{j \beta \sin(\theta)} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} J_n(\beta) e^{j n \theta} \]

Substituting \(\theta = 2\pi f_m t\) and extracting the real part yields Equation (2):

\[ s(t) = A \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} J_n(\beta) \cos\!\big(2\pi(f_c + n f_m)t\big) \]

Carson's Bandwidth Calculation (\(B_T \approx 2(\Delta f + f_{\max})\)):

  • Mono broadcast (\(f_{\max} = 15\text{ kHz}\), \(\Delta f = 75\text{ kHz}\)):
\[ B_{T,\text{mono}} = 2(75 + 15) = 180\text{ kHz} \]
  • Stereo multiplex (\(f_{\max} = 53\text{ kHz}\), \(\Delta f = 75\text{ kHz}\)):
\[ B_{T,\text{stereo}} = 2(75 + 53) = 256\text{ kHz} \]
  • Comparison with Broadcast Channel Spacing: Commercial FM channels are spaced by \(200\text{ kHz}\). The \(180\text{ kHz}\) mono transmission fits comfortably within the \(200\text{ kHz}\) channel allocation and is closest to this standard grid.

docs.title: 2. Carrier Nulls and Deviation Calibration
docs.text:
The amplitude of the center carrier line (\(f_c\)) is governed by the zero-order Bessel function \(J_0(\beta)\). The carrier completely disappears when \(J_0(\beta) = 0\). The first two positive roots of \(J_0(\beta)\) are:

\[ \beta_1 \approx 2.4048 \approx 2.405, \quad \beta_2 \approx 5.5201 \approx 5.520 \]

For a test tone of \(f_m = 1\text{ kHz}\), the corresponding frequency deviations are:

\[ \Delta f_1 = \beta_1 f_m = 2.405 \times 1\text{ kHz} = 2405\text{ Hz} \] \[ \Delta f_2 = \beta_2 f_m = 5.520 \times 1\text{ kHz} = 5520\text{ Hz} \]
  • Calibration Procedure: A pure \(1\text{ kHz}\) sinusoidal audio tone is fed into the FM transmitter while monitoring the RF output on a spectrum analyzer (or an SDR FFT sink). Starting from zero, the input audio amplitude is slowly increased until the center carrier peak at \(f_c\) drops into a sharp null and vanishes. At this exact point, \(\beta = 2.405\), confirming that the transmitter's frequency deviation is calibrated precisely to \(\Delta f = 2405\text{ Hz}\) without requiring a specialized deviation meter.

docs.title: 3. Discrete Phase Discriminator Linearity and Limits
docs.text:
The numerical discriminator computes the angular difference between two successive complex samples:

\[ y[n] = \arg\!\big(x[n] x^*[n-1]\big) = \arg\!\left(e^{j(\varphi[n] - \varphi[n-1])}\right) \]

Because the principal branch of \(\arg(\cdot)\) is constrained to \((-\pi, +\pi]\), the phase difference between consecutive samples must not wrap around:

\[ |\varphi[n] - \varphi[n-1]| = |k_f m[n]| < \pi \]

Since \(|m[n]| \le 1\), this condition reduces to:

\[ k_f = \frac{2\pi\Delta f}{f_s} < \pi \implies \Delta f < \frac{f_s}{2} \]
  • Maximum Detectable Deviation at \(f_s = 240\text{ kHz}\):
\[ \Delta f_{\max} = \frac{240\text{ kHz}}{2} = 120\text{ kHz} \]
  • Effect of Entering \(2\Delta f\) in Receiver Gain: The discriminator gain is \(\text{Gain} = \frac{f_s}{2\pi \Delta f_{\text{rx}}}\). If the receiver mistakenly assumes \(\Delta f_{\text{rx}} = 2\Delta f_{\text{actual}}\), the gain is halved:
\[ \hat{m}[n] = \frac{f_s}{2\pi (2\Delta f)} \cdot \left(\frac{2\pi\Delta f}{f_s} m[n]\right) = \frac{1}{2} m[n] \]

The output audio amplitude is attenuated by exactly \(50\%\) (a \(6.02\text{ dB}\) loss in volume), while remaining completely linear and free of distortion.

docs.title: 4. Comparison: Discriminator vs. PLL Frequency Detector
docs.text:
Comparison Metric Non-Coherent Discriminator (Quadrature Demod) Coherent PLL (PLL Frequency Detector) Design Parameters Only linear scaling gain: \(\text{Gain} = \frac{f_s}{2\pi\Delta f}\) Loop Bandwidth, damping factor, Min/Max Phase Performance Above Threshold Completely linear; parabolic output noise PSD (\(f^2\)) Identical to discriminator; linear frequency tracking Performance Near Threshold Exhibits sudden click impulses around \(\text{CNR} \approx 10\text{ dB}\) Threshold Extension: Delays threshold by \(2\text{ to }3\text{ dB}\) Carrier Offset Sensitivity Highly robust; carrier offset \(\delta f\) produces a harmless constant DC offset Vulnerable; if \(\delta f\) exceeds lock range, the loop loses lock entirely Computational Complexity Extremely low (one complex multiply + one \(\arg(\cdot)\)) Moderate to high (phase error, loop filter, NCO updates)
  • Why the PLL Threshold Advantage Increases with Large \(\beta\): When \(\beta \gg 1\), the Carson bandwidth \(B_T \approx 2\Delta f\) is vastly wider than the baseband information bandwidth \(W\). A non-coherent discriminator must accept all thermal noise across the entire transmission bandwidth \(B_T\). In contrast, the PLL acts as a dynamic tracking filter whose effective noise bandwidth \(B_L\) is matched only to the message rate (\(B_L \ll B_T\)). By rejecting out-of-band noise prior to nonlinear phase detection, the PLL suppresses phase slips, significantly improving threshold performance for wideband signals.

docs.title: 5. FM Improvement Trade-off Under Constant Received Power
docs.text:
Substituting \(\text{CNR} = \frac{P_c}{N_0 B_T}\) into Equation (8):

\[ \text{SNR}_o = \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{\Delta f}{W}\right)^2 \frac{B_T}{W} \left(\frac{P_c}{N_0 B_T}\right) = \frac{3}{2}\frac{(\Delta f)^2}{W^3}\frac{P_c}{N_0} \]

Assuming constant received carrier power \(P_c\) and noise density \(N_0\), doubling the frequency deviation (\(\Delta f \to 2\Delta f\)) yields:

\[ \text{SNR}_{o,\text{new}} = 4 \times \text{SNR}_{o,\text{old}} \implies 10\log_{10}(4) \approx 6.02\text{ dB improvement} \]
  • Threshold Power Shift: The threshold boundary occurs at a constant carrier-to-noise ratio:
\[ \text{CNR}_{\text{th}} = \frac{P_{c,\text{th}}}{N_0 B_T} = 10\text{ dB} = 10 \implies P_{c,\text{th}} = 10 N_0 B_T \]

Because \(B_T \approx 2(\Delta f + W)\), doubling \(\Delta f\) approximately doubles the occupied channel bandwidth \(B_T\) (for wideband FM). Consequently:

\[ \frac{P_{c,\text{th},\text{new}}}{P_{c,\text{th},\text{old}}} \approx \frac{B_{T,\text{new}}}{B_{T,\text{old}}} \approx 2 \implies 10\log_{10}(2) \approx 3.01\text{ dB} \]

To remain above the noise threshold, the transmitter must supply approximately \(3\text{ dB}\) more RF power.

docs.title: 6. Carrier Frequency Offset Analysis
docs.text:
If the received carrier possesses an unknown frequency offset \(\delta f\), the instantaneous frequency becomes:

\[ f_i(t) = f_c + \delta f + \Delta f\,m(t) \]

The discrete sample phase difference across interval \(T_s = 1/f_s\) is:

\[ \Delta \varphi[n] = 2\pi (f_i - f_c) T_s = \frac{2\pi}{f_s}\big(\delta f + \Delta f\,m[n]\big) \]

Applying the discriminator gain \(\text{Gain} = \frac{f_s}{2\pi\Delta f}\):

\[ \hat{m}[n] = \frac{f_s}{2\pi\Delta f} \cdot \frac{2\pi}{f_s}\big(\delta f + \Delta f\,m[n]\big) = m[n] + \frac{\delta f}{\Delta f} \]

The carrier offset appears as a pure, frequency-independent DC bias equal to \(\frac{\delta f}{\Delta f}\).

  • Numerical Offset Calculation at \(434\text{ MHz}\) (\(30\text{ ppm}\) tolerance):
\[ \delta f = 434\text{ MHz} \times 30 \times 10^{-6} = 13.02\text{ kHz} \]
  • Impact on a Narrowband Channel (\(B_T = 16\text{ kHz}\)): A narrowband channel filter centered at baseband has a one-sided passband edge of only:
\[ \frac{B_T}{2} = \frac{16\text{ kHz}}{2} = 8\text{ kHz} \]

Because \(\delta f = 13.02\text{ kHz}\) exceeds the \(8\text{ kHz}\) cutoff, the entire FM spectrum is shifted out of the filter's passband, causing severe attenuation, harmonic distortion, and complete loss of reception.

docs.title: Task 5: Risk Analysis and Failure Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Hardware Damage via Direct RF Overdrive (Critical Safety Risk)

  • Failure Mechanism: Connecting the PlutoSDR TX port directly to the RX port without the mandatory \(30\text{ dB}\) hardware attenuator, or setting the software internal attenuation to \(0\text{ dB}\).
  • Consequence: Power delivered to the receiver exceeds the maximum absolute damage rating (\(-10\text{ dBm}\)), permanently destroying the receiver's Low-Noise Amplifier (LNA).
  • Mitigation Protocol: Both team members must physically verify that the inline \(30\text{ dB}\) coaxial attenuator is connected to the RX port before executing the flowgraph, and verify Attenuation TX1 (dB) \(\ge 35\text{ dB}\) in PlutoSDR Sink.

2. Audio Distortion via Overly Constrained PLL Bandwidth

  • Failure Mechanism: Setting the Loop Bandwidth parameter of the PLL Frequency Detector too small (e.g., \(< 0.05\)) to suppress noise.
  • Consequence: The loop phase response becomes too slow to track rapid frequency deviations, causing cycle slips, loss of lock, and severe audio clipping/clicking.
  • Mitigation Protocol: Initialize with a conservative bandwidth (\(LB \approx 0.35\)) and reduce in small increments while monitoring the FFT sink and audio output.

3. De-emphasis Standard Mismatch

  • Failure Mechanism: Leaving the FM Deemphasis block at its default GNU Radio value of \(\tau = 75\ \mu\text{s}\) (North American / South Korean standard).
  • Consequence: Local Iranian and European FM broadcasts use a \(\tau = 50\ \mu\text{s}\) pre-emphasis curve; applying \(75\ \mu\text{s}\) excessively attenuates high frequencies, producing muffled audio.
  • Mitigation Protocol: Explicitly set the Tau parameter of FM Deemphasis to 50e-6 (\(50\ \mu\text{s}\)) per ITU-R BS.450 Region 1.
